blocks.x: Okay, it's going. You can give your name first.
My name is Albert Leroy Winn.
Oh, wait, let's try that again. The thing was slipping over. Try it once more.

Albert Leroy Winn. When were you born? I was born July the 29th, 1907, in New Orleans, Louisiana. And I might clarify it. In later years, some of the fellows called me Al. They sort of tagged the nickname on me, Al. They shortened it up a bit. But all the people that have known me for years, I'm still Albert.
Your last name, that's got the spelling too, because I've seen the E put on the end of it.
No, there's no E on it. W-Y-N-N.

It's usually that way, but a couple of times on some records, they put the E on the end. One of the old Brunswick's. Yeah. I think it was. The old Vocalion record. The ones you made with punch. Now, where were you born? In which part of town? Uptown or downtown?

I was born on Liberty Street between Tulane and Gravy. I don't remember the address. I thought it was, that's right on the edge of the district. At that time, the district was on Gravy Street. But this particular block on Liberty was a very nice block. Very nice, well kept and pretty flowers out front. I remember that much about it.
Up over between Perdido and Gravy or up that way is where the district was more.
Yeah, well the starting of it was at, at that time, the starting of it was at Liberty Street on Gravy. Yeah. And it went on up. I remember that much from it.
And Louis Armstrong was raised right up. Is that right? That neighborhood too.

I know Claris Williams, he had his music publishing company, well I guess it was a publishing company then, right around the corner on Tulane. Yeah. And I used to go around there and just hang around to hear the music and what not that was coming out. He would be playing, or different fathers would be in there playing and getting a thing. Well that was right around the corner on Tulane. Yeah.
I think 1100 and something is the address. I have some of the old sheet music published by P. Ronan. Is that right? Claris Williams, like Sister Kate and all that.

I remember that from a kid. And so I got, I was so interested in music at that time, I would always be hanging around out front to hear the sounds that were coming out. So he used to give me different little things to come on in and sweep the floor or something. And the Iroquois Theater on Ramport Street at that time, that was, that was the height. If I could get to the Iroquois on Sundays, that was it. You know, I would do anything to get some money to go to the Iroquois. And they had movies? They had movies, good westerns, and on Sundays they used to have live shows. Yeah. And one thing that stands out in my mind that when he wrote, My Mama's Baby Boy. My Mama's Baby Boy, one of those kind of things. And he would give us something, he would give all the kids that he knew, well here's a nickel now, when we come on you sing. He was promoting, from what I can recollect of it now, he was promoting songs, you know what I mean. And we would get in there and he would play it over and then we would join in on the course and start singing. My Mama's Baby Boy. Yeah. Used to whistle.
Everybody think it was a big hit in the old days. Oh yeah. It was a hit I guess too. In fact. Yeah. Can you remember the first music you ever heard? Did your parents play any instruments or sing?

Well, my father, he played a little trumpet. I never heard him play anything. I was quite young at that time. Yeah. But I understood that he played a little trumpet, you know, he was a trumpet player. My mother always, she loved music and everything, but she didn't play anything.
Probably sang good though I bet.

And dance, she liked dancing. She was crazy about dancing. I remember in my early days my parents separated and I was raised by my mother and I was very young and I remember on various occasions that she would say, now you sure you're alright to stay at home by yourself? I was quite young. Yeah. And I would say, yeah, well you go on out and enjoy yourself. And she would come back and tell me about that. One thing that stands out in my mind, it was a cabaret or something, Pete Lollis. It was, it was down the, downtown, not too far. Yeah.
About Murray and the Custom House or I don't know.

Yeah. And she was talking about Steve Lewis all the time, what a wonderful pianist he was. And unfortunately I never got to hear him or anything because I was a little young for that sort of thing. But she was always saying what a wonderful pianist he was and saying when you get to be a big boy I want you to be a musician and those kind of things.
When did you first take up music then?
I taken up music after I moved to Chicago. Yeah, that, we moved to Chicago possibly, it was in 19 or 20. I'm not, I'm not sure. It's very vague because I was still very young at that time.
About 1920?
About 1920 I would say. We'd be, be right.
Who did you study with or did you pick up the trombone yourself? Was that your first instrument?

No, I didn't pick up the trombone myself. In fact, my first love was the trumpet. I wanted, wanted a trumpet. But my family is very small. There's only about four of us in our immediate family. And my cousin is four years older than I am. So they wanted to start us to take in music at the same time. So he picked the trumpet. So it had to fall to me for the second choice. So my second choice was the trombone. I picked the trombone. And I, you know, stuck right with it. And my mother, it was quite a hardship on her to give me lessons and whatnot. I never will forget my first instrument. It was bought from Sears and Roebuck. Out of a catalog. I think it cost something like 1675. It was a beautiful instrument. A gautier. A gautier or something that had a French name. It was nickel plated. I couldn't afford the case or anything. So as I would go to take my music lesson, I'd have to get on the L. Because my lesson, I'd take my lessons on the south side from W.L. Jackson. He had a music school over here. And I would get on the L with the trombone all out, no case or nothing. People would be looking, but I didn't mind.
I was just a kid.
I didn't mind. So I started with Jackson for some time. He was, and by the way, he played the violin. He was a violin player, but he was a wonderful musician, a perfect knowledge of music.
Where was the studio?
The studio was in the 3100 block on State Street.
I think I've heard of the name Jackson.
Somebody else?
Yeah.

He had quite a few good teachers down there. But he himself, he was a terrific musician. But as far as the actual knowledge of the instrument, and later yes I found out that he didn't know. Because there were so many things that he started me off on wrong.
Yeah, all the fine points, yeah.

Yeah, for one thing, I'm left handed by a boy, you know. I didn't know. So, it was awkward for me to hold my trombone with the other hand. I said, well Mr. Jackson, I can hold it and work the slide better with my other hand. So he said, well turn it around. I said, okay, work it. Because of trombone, I mean you can turn it either hand. It don't make a lot of difference, but as you get in later life, it's very awkward. It looks awkward. Yeah. Other than, in reality there's really no difference, but it just looks awkward.
Did you learn it left handed then?
I learned trombone left handed. And it's a very unfortunate thing that I didn't even know that you had to put oil on the slide.
It was a slide, a breeze of sliding anyway, for about eight months.

And he had a lady there that was a teacher, she was a teacher and instructor in the school. So one day I happened to get her to give me my lessons, see. So she taking my horn to show me a passage, you know, how it should be played.
And she got the thing and she couldn't hardly move the slide.

She said, well when have you oiled it last? I said, oiled it last? I said, oiled it last? I said, I've never oiled it. She said, you mean you've never even put it, it was turning green, it was all canker. And then she went on to explain to me that you would have to put oil on the slide.
And how to take care of it.

But he has been not an instrumentalist on this particular instrument. He never told me to find points about the thing, so I didn't know anything about that. So from then on, I mean, I would try to get her every time I could. Because Mr. Jackson, musically, he was terrific. He was, but he was real cruel and real hard. I'll never forget his feet. He must have wore about a twelve or fourteen shoe. And if I would get the pattern of time wrong, which learning music you will, he would just take his feet and stamp right down on me. So I formed an awful dislike for him. An awful dislike for him. But I appreciated him running the rudiments. So I stayed with him for some time. But I would, as I say, I would always try and duck in this anyway possible to give this lady, because she could play the trauma. She could play the trauma. She was a lady, do you remember? I don't remember her name. No, it's been too long.
I don't remember her name.

So it was strictly one of those schools, you know, a bunch of kids. And they formed a little band, and we did one or two concerts after I'd been with them for a year. So, but I always wanted to play something with a sound. And naturally, just playing trombone parts, they don't sound like nothing. Even the little orchestrations that we would play in this little orchestra set up, there never was any melody, or any tune or anything connected to it. So my mother had been sacrificing and sending me to take these lessons. And after a couple of years, she said, well, when are you going to play a tune? So I tried to instill in her. I said, well, Mama, I'm playing the notes. You see the notes? She said, but it don't sound like nothing. There's no tune anything to it, see. So I would save up my little money and go down the line and heal in and buy orchestrations, which I thought would be the right thing. Well, when I'd get home with them and play the trombone parts, I could play the parts very easily. But there still wasn't any musical sound to it. It was just fill in parts, you know, the type of thing that trombone plays. So it had never once dawned on me that I could maybe just concentrate and play something from hearing it. So one day I happened to be out. I was doing the summer vacation out from school. And I was out looking for a job. I was way over north someplace. I don't have any idea what vicinity. But I went over to ask an ad for a porter and a drugstore. And I'm walking down the streets and I hear somebody playing a solo. The solo was Brunus' solo of Ten Loof Blue. Now I've had the record at home because I used to buy all those records and everything. But that was the first time that the idea dawned on me that anybody else could play that same thing other than the man that played it on the record. So I had this fellow, whoever it was, was just in the house and he was practicing this solo. I said, well if he can do it, I can go on home and do it. So consequently when I did get home that afternoon I picked out my own and found out I could play it just from here. Like that, you know. So from then on I could keep them happy around the house. I mean I could play some form of a melody or something, you know.
Tell me, when did you change over to right handed trombone then?

Oh I had been playing quite a few years. And how that come about, oh I had worked with Maureen and been all over the country and everything. And so I changed places with, I got tired of traveling. And there was another fellow here, a trombone artist, Lewis Taylor, he had never been out of Chicago. And he was with a very good band, a very good dance band. Let's see, what was the name of his band. I can't tell. But anyway, it was a very good outfit and the outfit was fellows like Les Hyde, Lionel Hampton, I don't know. They were all youngsters all the way up. But it was, so he had never been in a place, I say suppose we changed jobs. So we did. He went with Maureen and I went with them. So this band worked for a while until Les and Arnoldoff, George Arnoldoff and some of the boys got this chance to go to the coast. Well I had an offer to go along with them, one of those things, but my mother wouldn't let me go. She said no I don't want you going that far. So then I stayed around here. So there was a, Richard Jones was getting a band to go in a place on 33rd and Wabash. It was an amusement park with a dance pavilion, one of those diamond dance deals. And so he was getting this band. And it was just one of those things that was almost set for me. He had taken two or three of the boys that we'd come up with, Gabriel Washington, the drummer, and whatnot. The place was there, it was called Jarland Park. Of course the native Chicago's had another name for it, but we won't go into that.
You don't want to get that on the tape. Yeah.

And so I mean it was just one of those things that you figured I was just almost set for that because he was trying to get a bunch of the New Orleans playing musicians and whatnot. So at the last minute I was nixed out from this job. All my friends, it was quite embarrassing to me and everything, two or three of my real close boys that we'd come all up with, and we played about the same amount of music and everything. And he got a much older man who until this day at that time I know that I was more qualified for the job for what he was playing than this man was. So that just sort of broke my heart, you know, I just couldn't understand it. So one day about three weeks later, after they had opened on the job and everything was going very good, I ran into the clarinet player in the band who was a New Orleans boy, Dodo. He was a terrific clarinetist. Oh, I don't know him.
What was his last name? That's all I remember about Dodo.

He was terrific. One of the greatest of the old school clarinetists. So I ran into him on the streets and he started talking to me. And he just put it right on the line. He said, you know why you lost that job, why you didn't get that job. He went on to explain, he said, your playing would fit right in the front of me doing. I mean, you fit there, you belong there. He said, the man that we have, he don't play near as much as you playing. He don't fit. He said, but they say that you look awkward on the stands. They look like you're playing your instrument backwards. He said, it looks bad. As far as your actual playing and your musical ability, everything was all right. But they said, just look bad. So he gave me some advice. He said, the first chance you get, if I was you, I would turn that instrument around and start playing it right hand. And then, there's no excuse in it. So, that thing, it sunk in.
It sunk in.

I mean, it stayed with me because that was really a major disappointment in my life by not getting in that band. So I thought about what he had said. And shortly afterwards, I get a job to go with the group in South Bend, A Downer. So I had definitely made up my mind, I say. Because these fellas that I was going to work with, I mean, they were all new to me. I didn't know anything about them because it was different category of musicians and different fellas that I didn't know at that time. So I say, well, I'm going on this job and I'm going to try and make good. I'm going to try to play enough to get myself in their set and say, after I think that I'm in their set, I'm going to turn that instrument around one day and never turn it back again. And that's what I did. I went on out on this job and it was a terrific band, very good band. And the band was Tom Brown, who, he's in the Orleans Clanniers, two very, very good and wonderful pianists. William Barbee, you may have heard of him. He's on some of those records. Yeah, he made some records with Cine. Yeah, and he made some with me too.
Oh, I didn't know. Yeah, he's on some of those records with me.
So, I played my usual left hand way for about two or three months until I got set pretty good with the fellas. And one night I turned the horn around and I say, I never will turn it back again.
Well, it was almost like starting all over again. Did you practice at home?

Yeah, I would practice. We were living right up over the place that we were playing. We were playing in a cabaret and it was a hotel and everything. So, I would practice and I could play baritone, which at that time was a novelty up here, I mean getting off on the baritone at home. So, when I'd get tired or something would get too difficult for me to make on the slide with my left hand, I would pick up the baritone. And you'd use left hand on that, did you?
Well, no, the baritone I played at the right hand.

I played the baritone right hand, see. So, I stuck it on through this many times. I got disgusted. I said, well, there's no point in going through all this. But I never, if you notice on all the old pictures with Ma Rainey, all those Ma Rainey pictures and everything, if you notice, I'm left hand. Yeah, I'm playing left hand. I never noticed. I never noticed.
I never look at that though. It's funny I would have missed it.

Well, it's not a thing that the average layman would look at. I mean, it's just something you might look at a picture and say, well, something seems wrong, but you can't quite put your hand on it. Yeah.
I never felt like it. It doesn't bother you anymore now at all, I guess. You don't even think about it. Oh, no, I don't even think about it. You never know what to look at you.
I didn't even think about it. I mean, I went through that period. It probably take me six or eight months to get the feel of it.
And after that.
And then after that, I mean, it's kind of natural.
You still write, I guess, left-handed? Yeah.

Well, no, I don't write left-handed. That's the funny thing. When I went to school in Chicago, in those days, the teachers used to make you change hands. Now they don't do it with my kid. I mean, they say, if you left-handed, well, he's naturally left-handed like I was. And they don't change him. But when I come up here to school, the teachers changed me. I had started to write and left-handed because my first school was Fisk, and that was right around the corner from where I was living. And they closed the school because it was too near the district. Then they opened my McDonald 35 in Yarlins, and I went to McDonald. But down there, I mean, I started to write and left. But when I come up here to school, they start me going over. And now they don't do that to the kids. They say it's subject to retarded or something.
Yeah, sometimes it makes them stutter. Yeah. You never had any trouble, though, stuttering? No.
No, I never did. Uh-uh.

Well, some people were in fact, maybe others not. Can you tell me anything else about any other teachers you had or other trombone players you listened to? And maybe if you didn't study with them that you learned from them by...

Well, who has done more for me than anyone? Well, as I said, I was with Jackson for a few years, and he gave me all the fundamentals of things. But Preston Jackson was with the band. There was a place at 43rd and State Street upstairs. It was called the Red Mill. And, of course, I was on...it was just a dance hall. And it ran every Sunday. Every Sunday evening they would have matinee dances. And, of course, you couldn't get in there unless you had on long pants. Well, in those days, I mean, the boys, if you were underage, you still wore short pants. So I would conveniently arrange to...with some of the elder fellows to borrow our pants every Sunday. They would go up there and have this band. It was a terrific band. Oscar Young, he's a New Orleans boy, a trumpet player. He was very good. It was his band. And Preston... Oh, yes. Yeah, they later started calling him Bernie. I don't know if Bernie was his real name or what. But to everybody that had known him for years, it was Oscar. Oscar Young. Yeah, he's a rich man. And New Orleans, a very, very good trumpet player. And he had a terrific band.
Is he still around? No, he passed.

He passed about four years ago in Milwaukee. He was a terrific trumpet man. In fact, at that time, his band was considered the number two band in Chicago. Joe Oliver was first, and Bernie was number two. And Preston was playing with him, Preston Jackson. Yeah, he was right. And they were a perfect team. Well, they'd worked together for years and years. Preston and Oscar. And he always had a good band, terrific drummers. And, you know. So I would go to this Red Mill Hall, and I would just sit under Preston all day. I mean, I didn't go there for the play, but there was any dancing or anything. Yeah. I would just sit under the drum, right over on the side by him. And every chance I'd get out of it, try and talk with him. So, I told him that I was interested in trombone and had been taking him on the play. And I liked his way of playing. So I asked him if he would give me lessons. So he told me, well, I'm pretty busy now. I don't usually do those sort of things. But every Sunday I would ask him the same thing and keep happening. So he finally consented. He said, yeah, well, I'll teach you. So I started to taking lessons from Preston. And that's when I really learned what the trombone was about, you know. You know what I mean. Because he would give me everything that he knew and all his ideas and everything. He would just, well, he knew the instrument and he just passed it on to me. And he'd taken a liking to me so he would try. It got to be really a friendship relation. It wasn't no such thing as like you go over there and take your lesson for an hour, one of those kind of things. You'd come in, he wouldn't get out. And I got so carried away with Preston until, at that time, my family was living on the west side. And in Chicago at that time there were quite a few gang wars going on of the younger kids and that thing. If you lived on one part of town, you wasn't supposed to come over here for anything. And it was a funny thing, they could recognize you as being a stranger in the neighborhood. Just at the spur of the moment. So I had so much trouble coming over to Preston's house to take my lesson. I mean, sometime coming off the L, there would be a gang, this is my luck to walk into a gang, and they would either beat me up or run me back and one of those kind of things. So I had so much trouble that way and I kept after my mother. I said, let's move on the south side, you know, because they would give me the dickens. So eventually we moved right next door to where Preston was living, which was an ideal situation, which was cut and dry for me. So Preston was very tolerant with me. He just gave me everything he knew. He just taught me everything that he could about the home. So he finally left. He said, well, I'm going to New Orleans. He went back to New Orleans to stay for a year or two years. So he said that I will turn you over to the fellow that taught me. So he carried me over there and that turned out to be Roy Palmer, who was mine. He was one of the greatest of the traumas.
The technique that man had was just terrific.

I mean, he was just a natural traumas. So I finished up my studying with Roy. I went to Roy. Roy was just like Preston. I mean, he was just interested in kids and youngsters and he tried to pass on all his knowledge to me. But what year was that then when you studied the floor? That was probably in the early 20, in 21 or 22, somewhere around in there. Roy was a terrific technician on that floor.
He didn't make very many records. He made a few though, and you can hear him on some of them.

Yeah, the fellows used to say that, I never know if it would be a fact or something, but they used to say Roy was very lazy. They would say that he would come on a job and play like the Dickens probably for about 45 minutes and then he was ready to go to sleep or anything. Yeah, I heard that. But he was playing while he was playing. Yeah. And Roy was a fellow. I mean, I know this to be a fact that he didn't care anything about appearance. In those days bands used to wear tuxedas and whatnot. And I never will forget Roy used to come up to work. I remember several occasions I'd go around and wear his work. And then he had a tuxedo. It had turned green, the original color probably was black. I had one too. And he just soon put on a green shirt with a tuxedo. He was just that type, he was just what he was.
He used to work in the daytime too as a mechanic and all. I guess he'd be sleepy on a job. Yeah, and then he had quite a few kids.

I mean, Roy was a wonderful musician. I mean, it was fascinating to see how he could teach all those instruments. I mean, a lot of times I would go there early, you know. This time he would be teaching drums. And to my way of thinking now was correctly. I mean, he could pick up a drumstick and make it a beautiful, perfect roll. He could actually show you what he wanted you to do. That's the one thing that most of those teachers were like Mr. Jackson. He couldn't show you on your instrument how it should be done.
Roy played trombone. Yeah.

And just as good as he was on trombone. That's just as sad as he was on trumpet to my idea of thinking. His ideas on trumpet were very corny. I mean, my way of thinking. And he loved the trumpet. The trumpet was really his love. And after I got so that I could play, he had a marching band, a brass band around there. So he'd always put me on the trombone and he would play the trumpet. And I just didn't like his trumpet playing at all. It was really ratatirous, you know. But he had a terrific pair of lips. I mean, he could, for endurance and range, he had it all.

You know, Jolly Roe Martin and his Library of Congress records, he did a lot of talking and playing and, too. And he said Roy was his favorite trombonist. He said he was the greatest they had in New Orleans in the old days, too.
Roy was definitely one of the greatest. I understand that he made a... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ...
Okay, do you want to finish that up?
Let's just keep it off.
Okay, you were saying something about this record? Did Roy make it?
Yeah, Roy made a record, I understand, with Jelly Roll. I've never had to hear the record of High Society with Roy playing the Picou's clarinet solo. No, I don't think he did that. On the trombone.
No, I don't think he did that. No?

Well, there is supposed to be such a record that was made. Now, I know Roy can play it because he has played it for me. Lee Collins played it too on the trumpet. Yeah, well, it would be much easier on the trumpet, but on the trombone, that is something. Roy has played that This is Pretty. And there was a record, I remember at the time that it was made, maybe it didn't even come out or something, but I remember the...
You were talking about John Lindsay when he played bass?
Yeah, well you see, when he went to the Army he was a bass player.
So they carried a box around? Huh? They carried a box around?

Yeah, well that was in the Army. His daddy was a violin player. His brother's here now. Oh, his brother's still here? Yeah, his brother's here. He's a violin player. Joe Lindsay. Joe Lindsay's name. Where does he live in? Somewhere on the Prairie. Yeah, 40th around there. 40th to Prairie. Somewhere around. John Lindsay's, Joe Lindsay.
Joe was the one that's living.
That's living, yeah, John's dead. And when he came back he left here and went with the 8th Regiment band to the Army. And when he came back, he came back and Sergeant Tucker had the band.
He was a good trombone player then.

He was the 8th number one trombone player. But if he could get out of playing trombone he wouldn't play. If he wanted to play a job now he wouldn't play bass. He always wanted to play bass. But I made him play trombone.
He was on the records then too then? Yeah.

And you played trombone on the records? Yeah. He played trombone on all of my records that I made. Because that's the only way, if you wanted a man out of my band, at them times that's the only way you could get him, is to hire him or to hire me. Or get permission from me because he wouldn't play with you. See John was, the whole time, up until I lost my home, he lived with us. Him and his wife lived with us. Oh, he did? Yes. We lived together after we come up here. And the clarinet player was a male carrier. And he didn't depend on music for a living. What was his name again? Fred Palm. Fred Palm. E. E. Flat, saxophone player. And he'd tell you, he'd say, if you want me to play a gig with you at night, you'd call Willie up. Well, they'd say, I can go, I can go. And you'd have to call me, then I'd call Fred and tell Fred to go where he wanted. And I had another man from New Orleans, that probably, I don't know if you know, that I used in the band here. His name was, what's the drummer's name?
Huh? The drummer? Yeah. What was the band?
Rudy. Rudy. Rudy Richardson. No, I didn't know him. You didn't know him? No. Rudy Richardson.

Well, that's the man that practically inspirational, Lionel Hampton playing cellophones. This boy played cellophones. And all those men, like we used on that, the Chinese job we used, well I didn't use, what's it called, on drums, I used, what's the boy's name, that died in, Ernest Parker. I used him. Ernest Parker, man. Yeah, he's from Minneapolis. He was a good drummer too. And on all the records that Miney made, that's when he didn't use, what did you say they call it? What did you say the current player was that you, what's he last night was sick?
Lee Collins. Lee Collins.
See, he switched between me, when he get mad at me, tell me that I should have got Lee Collins in the house. The player now said, well, you get a Lee Collins. Lee Collins. Yeah.
Lee Collins. Lee Collins. Lee Collins. Lee Collins. Lee Collins. Lee Collins.

Yeah. Lee Collins. Lee Collins. Yeah. No, he was a, no, wait a minute, I can't think of the, but we cut, I cut, I think, four, four numbers, before, I made, I recorded, the boy called blues, and squeezed me. Bull Hog on one side and squeezed me is on the other.
That was on the Black Patty.

Black Patty. Now the other records that we made was for Melrose. We made them at Chicago, what is it, Chicago Avenue in the Lake, out there, 17th floor. That's where we made them. But Mr. Melrose, his brother was over there. The old Melrose wasn't there, he said.
Walter Melrose.
Yes, Walter was the oldest one, wasn't he?
Yes, I think so. And the young one was the blonde head. There was Lester. Yeah. And there was the piano player, Frank Melrose.

Well, I think we did business with the heavy something, the blonde, Connie blonde had one. Mr. Melrose himself was thin, wasn't he, a little thin. Well, that's who he made these last records with until we went down there to cut full numbers, two records. And that stuff is all in storage, I couldn't give you that because I made manuscripts of the numbers. And then we was talking about it last night. And in making these numbers, he had a four-boy introduction on one. And that's the number he wanted to cut first, was his own music. And I told him in rehearsal, we were rehearsing over here on Prairie, and 52nd Street. And I told him, I said, we'll have to change that trombone number, that trombone note. And he got sold with me and said that it was his music and he wanted it like he wanted. So we went down to record this. So the man, the, he hit with us down, played with us and went on so and so with us until he told us to hit. Well, the hit made the introduction. We went on and started the first string of the number. And after we started, the man see, we knew what we had. He stopped us. He said, well, to save time, he says, you boys will have to change that trombone number, the trombone note in there. And mine got bad with him. And they had a horse. And the man went and got a sheet of paper, pencil, come back. Mine got up from the piano, grabbed his music and he said, if that's the way you want it, he says, oh, you pack up. And we came on out of the studio. We didn't make those, and he had some nice numbers. No, we had some nice numbers. Lee Collins made them. Yeah. Whatever it was, because I met somebody on 47 in Michigan after coming from the Rican and they told me Lee Collins and told me who, I think he had Dominic, Dominic and Lee Collins is the man made him.
Well, that Boer Hog Blues and the Squeeze Me, do you remember just who was on that? Was that the same group you told about with John Lindsay? Yeah.
That's the same group.
That was on the Boer Hog.
Yeah. That was, well that wasn't the same group that made the number, because she was with, yeah.
Oh, your wife played on that record too?

Yeah, no, not on the record. We played, that was the same band that played the number, but she didn't play on the record. No, Mine played on the record. He played on the record. Yeah, that's the, that's the, it squeezed me. It squeezed me in that one. And since I've lost all my stuff, see when I come out of 4914 Forestville, I was practically stranded, and all that stuff was lost in storage, and I've been trying to get a record, and I haven't been able to get that Black Patty yet, and I've sent all the way to New York. I lost all that stuff in storage. Oh, for sure. Now, I think Baby Dots has got one. There's two or three of the musicians that's got them around here, and they wouldn't let me get my hands on them. They wouldn't let me even see them.
If Baby's got it, he wouldn't let me see it. I don't know that I, I don't believe Baby has one. I've never seen it over there.
Yeah, Mine.

No? Well, why did you get it at that? First, I found an old cracked copy years ago. I had a crack all the way up to the center. Yeah. And I gave that away. It would hardly play. I straight had to break my needle. Yeah.
I gave it to some kid from California.

One begged me for it, and I gave it to him. Uh-huh. And then I found another one in Chicago a few years ago, and mine is pretty worn. Sometime maybe I can make a copy of it for you. Yeah. I'll try it.
Well, this company went out of business.
This company was on Madison Street. They were on Madison. Yeah, they were on Madison.
Yeah, they were on Madison.
Yeah, they were on Madison.
Yeah, they were on Madison. Yeah, they were on Madison. I think around 10 hundred, somewheres out there. That's where you made the record. That's where we made the record. Yeah.
And someday I'll try to get a copy of that for you.

Yeah. And that's one of those records that I was telling you where the instruments did the talking. Johnny played on his trombone, this thing was a hog grunting while the band played. Oh, right. See, that's what made the number go, see. And the squeeze me was my, now the squeeze me number, I don't know who that number was. That wasn't my original number. No, it was I think Clarence Williams and Fats Waller.
Yeah, Fats Waller, I think it was Fats Waller.

And some of them got together on it. Clarence Williams or some of them got together. And I got the numbers. And I had been down to the dancing class down there. And what was the piano player's name at the dance that got me the job down there? Clarence Williams.
Piano player?
Clarence Williams. He left him, went to New York to see, you heard of him? Yes, I know him.
I know him.

You know him personally. Well he's the one that wanted me to record all of this stuff. And he had done, down in Liszt I guess he had somewhere as long about eight or ten numbers that he wanted me to record. Because he said that he'd never heard nobody play them numbers like that. Well you see, when I come in Chicago, I was to go to work for him when he was downtown at Boucher's place, see? Yes. See, but I didn't go down there, see? And when he come out to the Owls Theater, you know he stayed at the Owls Theater a long time. He had a band there too. Clarence Williams? Clarence Jones.
Clarence Jones.
Oh, Clarence Jones. Yeah. Well he went to, you should, Clarence Jones? Clarence Williams, what?
Clarence Williams was in the U.
Yeah. He had a publishing house here down on State, about 35th and State Street for a while. Who? Clarence Williams.
Clarence Williams.
He's in the other one?

No, he had a place, no. That was real early though, maybe before you moved here. 4th Street, baby, right by Beckers. Huh? Right where Rod Pomer was staying, by Beckers. Clarence Williams, yeah. Yeah, Clarence Williams. He had six people working for him in that place.
I thought you were in Clarence Jones.
No, Clarence Williams.
One time Clarence Williams did have a publishing house here at your music store.

Oh yeah. 44th and State. And he had six people working for him. And most of them ranges, and you would be surprised to think of the business that he did in that place with six people working. A lot of business. Sending music, just mailing music all over the country. See? Ain't but the one thing, he had a little bad luck, mishap along with it. Now he's got back on his feet again, last time I heard from him.
This is in New York.
Yeah, he's doing good.

Oh, I was going to ask you, in New Orleans, I don't want to keep you in any longer because everybody wants to get to bed. Roy Palmer, where did he live? Near you, up at 6th Street, around? No, he stayed up Protection Levy.
Way up around Carlton. Around Carlton, the other side of St. Charles.
So maybe he moved down to your neighborhood? No, never did he.

He stayed up in that part of the country, up in that part of the city. Because most of the work that he got was two long grounds that we worked at up there. That's the one that helped us a lot. He knew the people up there, see? And after we got straightened out and, as I told you, could play, that's where we made our greatest reputation up there. Because then most of the time, I hadn't come down to the district where I met Wade Whaley and we had to sign it. We was using Bechet up there, there, see? Oh, yeah. And we had to put long pants in here for him to use him up there, because Bechet was in short pants still. But outside of that, Roy never did come downtown. He never did stay down.
One more question about the, did you ever play any parades very much in New Orleans?
Played the most, the first parades that I made in New Orleans was from, what's the younger player's name? It's a bit of a thing, you can't think of nobody.
Well, Freddie Keppert or? No. Manuel Perrinas? Henry Allen. Oh, Henry Allen.
From Oven-Algeous.
Oven-Algeous. You heard of Henry? Yes. That was Henry Allen, young Henry Allen's father.

Yeah, that was his father. Oh, yeah. And his son, the one that's playing now, used to walk between us and hold both of us's horn under one arm. He'd hold his daddy's horn under one hand when we wasn't playing, and under his arm, and he'd hold mine under the other. He was about nine years old then, see? And after I played over there, and then we got all that work from Seussbury, Protection Levy, all of that, see? And all the summer long we were just playing parades up there for different lodges.
Yeah.

Then after I got in the district, as I told you, Zoo was playing trombone in P. Ronce's band. And most of the musicians from downtown, they didn't like Creoles, they didn't like nobody, stayed uptown, because I didn't speak French, see? And Manuel Perez, that's a trumpet player? Yes, that's right. That had the Exsulsa, that was the Exsulsa? Sometime the Enruid band. Enruid, Enruid band. And he had Joe playing trumpet with him. And he was playing cornet. And Sue Zoo was his trombone player. Zoo was one trombone player, and Eddie Atkins was the other, too. You know those two good men right there, you heard Eddie Atkins was good, too, see? And they put me in the band. So that made me the third trombone player, third trumpet player in the band, then I got all of that work with that band work. And then I found myself, after I got in that band from downtown, I found myself playing in the district at night, and just taking my horn, and taking my band uniform, and going to the parade and parade all day long. And just every day, there was a parade we had. Either that or somebody did. You see, around then we... They still had those funerals. Yeah, we had to play for the courts. They still do. That's right. Any time, they do that yet?

Well, they still do, yes. They still do that. Every Sunday there'll be a parade in the summertime. Two weeks ago, before I came up, there were three parades that Sunday. Is that so? Yeah. And they still bury with the band? Yes. Not so many, but maybe one a week there'll be a few... There are lodges and things, good clubs.
They bury with a band. You see, I belong to the Tanninist Social Club, and I belong to the Bulls.

Oh, yes. The Bulls is uptown. They sold out under the Elks. They sold out under the Elks. It's on the Dan Neal and the... And the Lions is downtown yet? I'm not sure about the Lions. I don't remember. They were French.
I think they were down by the Economy Hall.
Yeah, down there on Dumaine or something.
Dumaine, somewhere it's down there, see.
It's an undertaking part.
Clayborne, somewhere around Clayborne.
Down near Clayborne and Dumaine, but it's an undertaking part. Yeah. Oh, one other question. Did you ever hear Bunk Johnson, did you ever hear him play?
Bunk Johnson? Why, Bunk, why, he started to play him. Bunk started to play him when Eddie Bolden had a band.
Yeah. Did you ever hear Bolden?

Oh, yes. But I was so small then, see. And his mother didn't want him to play. So Bolden and them begged his mother and they took him on a job. And Bolden used to bring his clothes for him to dress him. And take him back home and put him in his knee pants and send him home. He lived in my neighborhood at Pellis City and Cronolette.
The Bunk Dead. Yeah.

When he was little. And his mother, he'd make his mother mad or something. When he was out there playing, she'd make him come in. We'd be out there playing Marvels in the street. He'd have to stamp on the fence and look at us. See. And he kept on, kept on until after he grew up. He still kept to that horn. When his mother got so that let him go. So he didn't stop uptown at all for no musicians. He went downtown. He got in with some band downtown. I don't know what that band was named. But Bunk come in and went out so quick until as I try to figure the music world as it's gone so poor today. I didn't hardly realize that Bunk had been in the music business until we just forgot it. Because he come up so, all of a sudden Bunk was the greatest trumpet player in the world. He really thought he was great. Then he went right down and he left New Orleans and went to somewhere as in Mississippi on a rice farm and stayed down there until Esquire. Got him. Well now I was to make that concert he made, Esquire made, see, in New York.
Oh yes.
Yeah. They wanted me and I wouldn't even go. Because they had set up. Now they went down there and bought Bunk I think a set of teeth. And wait until he trained himself to them, see.
They bought him a suit of clothes. How did Bunk play when he was young?

Young? Yeah. He was, what the time that he was, he flew right straight on up there. He was just great. Just great. But as suddenly as it looked like it just was a flash, it just looked like he come up and played all of a sudden and everybody in the Orleans just went crazy. Then after a while we ain't got no Bunk. It was a funny thing. And he never come back no more.
Never came back.
He never come back. But this time they tell me they took him to New York. When was that? It was about five?
Oh, in 1945. I was there in New York when he was there.

Yeah, yeah. Well they tell me he was all right. Well, what he wanted to do, he was kind of fanatic. He was very thin. At the time that he was coming up and he was kind of flighty like, see. He wanted certain musicians I guess that he'd come in with so it seemed like after that concert was that he got an agent. I don't know who booked him in New York but they got Bechet for him and they formed a band
and went to Los Angeles. I just wondered how Bunk played when he was real young. Did you ever hear him play parades? How was he on parades?
Well I don't know about parades. The most I knew about him was that dance band and most of those men were old men. Yeah. And he played at the Carpenters Hall downtown.
The Carpenters Hall.
Yeah, yeah. He always played. He didn't play uptown at all. All that band stayed downtown, see. And as I said they were all French.
Yeah, the Superior Band I think.
Yeah, the Superior Band was the name of the band. That was the band.
Do you remember anything about Bolden? And I'm going to stop talking to you. I'm not going to make you talk anymore. If you can just tell a little bit about Bolden if you remember when you heard him.

Just enough to know that about, I don't know how long it was, but just about the time I got, I wasn't old enough to play then, see. Yeah. I played at a place called the Lincoln Park. That's around Carlton Avenue. Yeah. It used to have Buddy Bolden, used to go up in a balloon. Man used to go up in a balloon because it was a parish. Buddy Barclay that was.
Buddy Barclay, that's what it was.
Yeah. Buddy Barclay, that's what it was.
I heard it. I never saw it, but I heard it.

Yeah. Well, he was playing an advertisement for that Lincoln Park, for that Sunday, at Melkameen and Drys. Everybody, what was that, the market? It used to be the market. No, the old Drys market. It's still there. It's still there? Yeah, well, there's all Melkameen. Well, he blew his brains out right there.
Just playing an advertisement for the Lincoln Park. In a puncture wagon.
In a wagon.
Yeah.

Yeah, that's what they used to advertise. Yeah, that's right. In a puncture wagon, horse and wagon. And he never was no more good. He'd take him sick and they'd take him to the hospital. There was no good. And shortly after that, he died. But I didn't realize, but they said, after Freddie come up and started playing, they said, we tried to say Freddie was great, but they said he was the greatest one that there was. Bowling. Bowling, that's right. He was the greatest. He could make the highest notes.
You think Freddie Keppert was about the greatest you ever remember hearing though now?
Yeah. That is for playing ragtime music.
No, ragtime.

Yeah, rag, we didn't call it no jazz then. You see, because everything was Scott Joplin then. Yeah. See, and we played all, any time any musician could play Scott Joplin's, I've got the books. I have the books. There's twelve numbers in the books, isn't there? Well every one of Scott Joplin's numbers, from Maple Leaf Ray to Cascade, and any musician, any trumpet player could play Cascade, he was a musician of mine.
Yeah.
And that's what Freddie Keppert played.
Would you like Keppert better than Joe Oliver?

Well, it's just like one of those things that, that I figured that although that me and Joe turned out to be the best friend, and when he got sick here on his last laps, I held his job down at the plantation for him for about six months, and did my work too, because he was unable to work. You see, he had a drummer in there by the name of, this drummer, went back in the orange. Oh, Paul Barber.
Paul Barber. Yeah, I know. He was racing one day. I'm a good friend of mine.
Yeah, Paul Barber was racing, and they had rehearsal, and they come out back on Calumet Avenue, and run, and Joe fell. Oh, really? And that's the cause of his death today.
Had a race.

Had a race. Yeah, him and Paul, they run. And he wasn't able, so he called my wife up and asked me to come down, and I held the job over there for him and Joe Glazer. Joe Glazer had the place. That's right, Joe Glazer.
Yeah, that's right.

And so I held the job for Joe, and me and Joe was good friends, because Freddie was only a friend, I figure like on business association with Freddie, because he did work in my lawn grounds for me, see. I owned a pleasure ground and dance and lawn parties and things, and I give their band more credit of bringing people into place, see, other than that. And then, after we come here, why, then I found out that he was with Charlie Cook, and I knew Charlie Cook from Texas, see, before we ever come into New Orleans, and he stopped in New Orleans a while, and then he went on back to Texas, and then he come on this part of the country and made good, see. But other than that, why, in playing, why, I think Freddie's just about as great as he comes.

Sorry, I never got to hearing. Yeah. Well, I want to take more of your time, because I know you have to get up early. Yeah. So I certainly appreciate your interview and taking all this time. Yeah. I'll just run this on, speak this on, and I'll pack up.
Okay, that's going again.
Yeah, so...
We were talking about the Savoy...

Yeah, they were working at the Savoy then. So I just got in town, well, actually, they're the first ones that knew I was back and whatnot. They told me their program, and they were working up there and everything. So they say, I never belonged to the New York local, you know. In fact, at that time, I was under the impression I didn't belong to any local because I hadn't paid any dues in Chicago for a period of five years, four or five years. So they say, well, we've got to arrange it, we've got to smuggle you in here, and one of those things. So they were having the breakfast dances at Small's. So I went there and I ran into a lot of the Chicago musicians at the Newman. It was strictly professional breakfast dances, you know. And everybody, here's old Al, come on and play. So I get up to play, and I get up and blow some with them. I'm so happy and so thrilled to be back. And as it would happen, the Union man was in there, which was... Minton was there at that time. Minton was there, Minton. And it was near election. He and Peekaboo Jimmy was running against Minton, see. And so they heard me. And Tom and Bashe come and say, that's the worst thing you could have ever done. And they go, well I'm just glad to be back home and out having fun and seeing the boys and anxious to play because I mean the only things that I'd heard from over here was the canned music, you know. So it was a natural mistake. So that sort of cramped things with the Union. Come to find out, I couldn't, I rode out here. I had all kind of jobs in New York. But I went to the Cotton Club with Cal. Fletcher warned me. But my heart was set on going with Bashe and Tommy. In fact, we would have rehearsals every day and those rehearsals were so much in job. And we would sit up there and rehearse all day long, you know, and drink root beer. There was a root beer place. You could get a gallon of root beer for about fifteen cents. And it was just fascinating. But due to the fact that Peekaboo Jimmy was running against Minton for his job, Peekaboo couldn't give me the pass to do anything. I mean Minton couldn't because Peekaboo would tell, would go downtown and tell everything. And so it sums down. So I tried to join outright to say, well, first you got to get a release from Chicago. I write that, yeah.
They said, no, you're still originally a member of Chicago.

I couldn't start a regular job on the, on the, on the, and yet I hadn't paid any dues. And so it was just one of those things. I mean everybody tried to straighten it because during that time, Bushbaum was in and he knew me. And he tried his best, but he said, no, you got to stay that waiting period out. Well, Louis Russell had a very good band at that time. Hickey was with him and everything. Well, Louis was just gigging around. So I made a few dates with them. And Louis said, well, you can come on in the band as a regular member anytime you like to. But by me not being able to take a regular job, it's sort of just taking all the spirit out. I even, uh, taking one of those dancing schools, I say, well, maybe I can go down there. In those days you could get, they work you, work you like, like the Dickens. But I said, maybe I can hide out down there for a while and keep me going until I get, uh, my status straightened out. But men finally come down there and say, Al, I don't want to cause any trouble. Say, but the next time I catch you, boy, I got to turn in. There's nothing I can do but turn in. So I got disgusted and said, well, I'll come on out to Chicago. So I'll come on out here.
Well, we got the end of that story. And that's just something else that you think ought to be told, especially?

Well, there's nothing other than that when I come to Chicago. Nothing very much was happening here. I went with Jesse Stone. We finally got a band together and opened a new spot here, the Club Morocco. But they had a lot of hometown boys that didn't want to go any place. It was discontented. Never the type of Jimmy Noon now. Yeah, Jimmy Noon eventually went in the same place. So, uh, in the meantime, I leave Jimmy Stone and go with Carol Dixon as a replacement at the Grand Terrace when Earl would go out on the road. So I went down there and worked. And then Jimmy Noon got this job in the Club Morocco. So I went with Jimmy. And I worked with him until I joined Fletcher. I joined Fletcher Henderson. And I was with him until the time he broke up his band going with Benny Goodman.
Oh, yeah.
He broke up the band in Boston. And he went with Benny. So I come back and joined Jimmy Noon again at another place down at 35th Street. The Platinum Lounge, maybe?
No, the Platinum Lounge.
That was on Vincennes.
Oh, yeah.
That's where I came from. 35th and State. It was the same spot that I'd worked in. Cabin Inn, they called it. Oh, yeah, sure.
It moved from down.
It used to be in the 34th block.
Yeah. It was the Death Blocker movement.

Yeah. So I worked with Jimmy until that fall. We were on WBBM there, broadcasting. And it was, he had a big band there. It was a nice, happy relationship. Jimmy was one of another one of those grand leaders. He was one of the most remarkable fellows you ever want to work with.
Yeah, he was wonderful, too. Wonderful, wonderful fellow. I knew him fairly well. I heard him a few times.

And one thing stands out in my mind about him, his love for food. He loved to eat. Yep. And when he wasn't eating, he would like to talk about it. He would have just got up from dinner and come to work, and he's telling you what he had for dinner in my hands. He'd go into all details, whatever little thing he had. And he just got there, and we just hit in the first setting. He would call the waitress, have me a half a chicken right at intermission. We'd take an intermission about half an hour after we started, because we had to get ready for the broadcast. And he would be all ready to eat all over. He was terrific. Wonderful to work with. Never, never no hassle either way.
Yeah, he was a nice fellow.
I found that all your great musicians were really wonderful fellows.
I think so, too. It was funny.
And the little fellows that you don't, the class amount to too much.
They're the backbriters.
Those are the ones that try to make life miserable and hard for everybody. One of the unfortunate situations of life.
Well, I certainly enjoyed the interview with you, and I want to thank you again.
Well, it's a pleasure. I'm always willing and available. Anything I can do.
Thank you, and I certainly appreciate it. Thank you.
Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.
